chapters.n: Joseph Smith explains why he is writing: hostile, distorted stories about him and the Church were spreading, and he wants honest seekers to have the facts in his own words. This history was begun in 1838 and is one of several accounts he gave of his early experiences.
Joseph promises to tell the events truthfully, writing in 1838, eight years after the Church was organized on April 6, 1830.

f.g: Joseph began dictating this history in 1838 in Far West, Missouri; it was first published in 1842 in Nauvoo.

f.w: the organization of the said Church

chapters.n: Joseph was born on December 23, 1805, in Sharon, Vermont. His family moved to Palmyra, New York, around 1816, then to nearby Manchester. Like many New England families, the Smiths moved west seeking better farmland after crop failures.

f.g: A small farming town in Windsor County, Vermont.
A village in western New York on the newly built Erie Canal route.

chapters.n: Joseph lists the eleven members of his family: his parents, Joseph Sr. and Lucy Mack Smith, and their nine living children. His oldest brother Alvin died in 1823 — a loss the family felt deeply.

In about 1820, a wave of religious revivals swept the area — part of what historians call the Second Great Awakening. Methodists, Presbyterians, and Baptists competed for converts, causing excitement and division.
Joseph notes that the warm feelings at conversion soon gave way to bitter competition. Ministers and converts argued over opinions, and the love they had professed seemed to vanish.

f.g: leave one by one, as from a line.

chapters.n: Joseph was fourteen. Part of his family — his mother, brothers Hyrum and Samuel, and sister Sophronia — joined the Presbyterian church.
The religious excitement troubled Joseph deeply. He attended various meetings and leaned toward the Methodists, but as a young, inexperienced boy he could not tell which church was right.
The noise and arguing were constant. Each church tried hard to prove the others wrong, using both genuine reasoning and clever but misleading arguments.
Amid the “war of words,” Joseph asks the questions that will lead to the First Vision: Which church is right? Are they all wrong? And how can I know? Honest questions open the way to revelation.
While struggling, Joseph reads James 1:5 — if you lack wisdom, ask God, who gives generously and does not scold. This single verse changes the course of his life.

f.w: If any of you lack wisdom, let him ask of God

chapters.n: The verse strikes Joseph with great power. He realizes that he needs God’s wisdom, especially since ministers interpreted the Bible so differently that the Bible alone could not settle his question.

f.w: with more power to the heart of man

chapters.n: Joseph concludes he must either stay confused or do as James says — ask God. Trusting the promise that God gives liberally and without scolding, he decides to “venture.”

f.g: dare to try, take the risk.

chapters.n: Joseph goes into the woods near his home on a clear morning in early spring 1820. It is his first attempt to pray out loud. The place is now known as the Sacred Grove.

f.g: A grove of trees near the Smith family farm in Manchester, New York, now called the Sacred Grove.

chapters.n: As soon as Joseph begins to pray, a terrifying power seizes him, binds his tongue, and surrounds him with thick darkness. He feels he is about to be destroyed.
Using all his strength, Joseph calls on God to save him from this real, unseen enemy. Just as he is about to give up, a pillar of light brighter than the sun descends upon him.

f.w: some actual being from the unseen world

chapters.n: The light frees him. He sees two glorious Personages in the air. One calls him by name and introduces the other: “This is My Beloved Son. Hear Him!” Latter-day Saints understand these to be God the Father and Jesus Christ.

f.w: This is My Beloved Son. Hear Him!

chapters.n: Joseph’s purpose was to learn which church to join. As soon as he can speak, he asks — never having considered that all of them might be wrong.

f.w: which of all the sects was right

chapters.n: He is told to join none, because they had all strayed. The Lord quotes Isaiah and Paul: people honor Him with words, teach human ideas as doctrine, and have a form of godliness while denying its power. The criticism is of creeds and corruption, not of sincere individuals’ goodness.

f.w: they draw near to me with their lips
having a form of godliness, but they deny the power thereof

f.g: formal statements of belief adopted by churches.

chapters.n: After the vision Joseph finds himself on his back, weak, and goes home. He tells his mother simply that he has learned Presbyterianism isn’t true. He reflects that the adversary seemed to know early that he would disturb Satan’s kingdom.

f.w: many other things did he say unto me, which I cannot write
f.g: Joseph’s other accounts of the First Vision (1832, 1835, 1842) add details, including the forgiveness of his sins.

chapters.n: A few days later Joseph tells a Methodist preacher about the vision. The preacher scorns it, saying visions and revelations ended with the apostles.

f.w: all such things had ceased with the apostles

chapters.n: Telling his story stirs up prejudice and persecution. Though Joseph is an unknown teenager from a poor family, respected men across the churches unite in opposing him.

f.g: people who profess or claim religious faith — church members.

chapters.n: Joseph marvels that a poor, obscure boy who had to work daily just to get by would attract such bitter opposition from prominent religious leaders. It caused him real sorrow.
Joseph compares himself to the Apostle Paul, who testified before King Agrippa of his vision of light and a voice. Though mocked, Paul knew what he had seen, and persecution could not change it.

f.g: he was insane — the charge Festus made against Paul (Acts 26:24).

chapters.n: Joseph bears his own testimony: he truly saw a light and two Personages who spoke to him. He cannot deny it without offending God. This is one of the most direct testimonies in all scripture.

f.w: who am I that I can withstand God
I knew it, and I knew that God knew it

chapters.n: Joseph is satisfied that he should not join any church but wait for further direction. He has proved James’s promise true.
For three years Joseph goes about his ordinary work while being persecuted by religious and nonreligious people alike for maintaining that he had seen a vision.

Joseph candidly admits that as a teenager he made foolish mistakes and showed youthful weakness — not serious sins, but lightheartedness and keeping cheerful company unsuited to someone called of God. His honesty shows prophets are human.
Feeling condemned for his weaknesses, on the night of September 21, 1823, Joseph prays for forgiveness and to know his standing before God, fully trusting he will receive an answer.

f.w: my state and standing before him

chapters.n: While he prays, his room fills with light brighter than noon, and a personage appears beside his bed, standing in the air.
The messenger wears a brilliantly white robe, whiter than anything on earth. Joseph carefully describes the visible details of his appearance.
The messenger’s whole person shines, his face like lightning. Joseph is frightened at first, but the fear soon leaves him.
The messenger introduces himself as Moroni, sent from God’s presence. God has a work for Joseph, and his name will be spoken of for good and evil among all nations — a prophecy still being fulfilled.

f.g: The last Book of Mormon prophet, who buried the plates around AD 421 (Moroni 10:1-2) and returned as a resurrected messenger.

f.w: good and evil spoken of among all people

chapters.n: Moroni tells of a book on gold plates recording the ancient inhabitants of the Americas and their origins, containing the fulness of the gospel as Jesus taught it to them.

f.w: the fulness of the everlasting Gospel

chapters.n: With the plates were two seer stones set in silver bows and fastened to a breastplate — the Urim and Thummim — prepared by God for translation. Possessing and using them is what made someone a “seer.”
Moroni quotes Old Testament prophecies, beginning with Malachi 3 and 4, wording some verses differently from the King James Bible.
Moroni’s version of Malachi 4:1: the coming day will burn the proud and wicked like stubble — “they that come shall burn them,” suggesting heavenly beings accompanying the Lord.

f.g: dry stalks left after harvest, which burn quickly.
no ancestors or descendants — total destruction.

chapters.n: Moroni’s version of Malachi 4:5: God will reveal the priesthood by Elijah before the Lord’s great day. Elijah came to the Kirtland Temple on April 3, 1836, restoring the sealing keys.
Moroni’s version of Malachi 4:6: Elijah will plant in children’s hearts the promises made to their ancestors. Without this sealing work for families, the earth would be wasted at Christ’s coming.

f.w: the promises made to the fathers

chapters.n: Moroni also quotes Isaiah 11, saying it is about to be fulfilled, and Acts 3:22-23 about the prophet like Moses — identified as Christ. Those who will not hear Him will soon be cut off.
Moroni quotes Joel 2:28-32 — God will pour out His Spirit on all flesh — saying it will soon be fulfilled, along with the “fulness of the Gentiles.”
Joseph must not show the plates or the Urim and Thummim except to those he is commanded to show, or he will be destroyed. In vision he sees exactly where the plates are buried.

f.w: only to those to whom I should be commanded

chapters.n: The light gathers around Moroni, and he ascends through what looks like a channel into heaven, leaving the room dark again.
As Joseph lies wondering, the room grows light again, and Moroni returns.
Moroni repeats everything word for word, then adds warnings of great judgments — famine, war, and disease — coming upon the earth in this generation.

Moroni comes a third time, repeats it all, and adds a caution: because the Smiths are poor, Satan will tempt Joseph to seek the plates for money. Joseph must seek only to glorify God and build His kingdom.
After Moroni’s third departure, a rooster crows — the visits had taken the whole night.
Exhausted, Joseph cannot work. His father sends him home, but while climbing a fence he collapses unconscious.
Joseph wakes to Moroni calling his name. Moroni repeats his message a fourth time and commands Joseph to tell his father.
Joseph obeys. His father immediately affirms it is from God and tells him to do as commanded. Joseph goes to the hill and recognizes the place at once.

f.g: Joseph Smith Sr. believed his son from the start and later became the Church’s first Patriarch.

chapters.n: Near Manchester is a large hill, the highest around. On its west side, under a large rounded stone, lay the plates in a stone box. This hill is now called Cumorah.

f.g: Now known as the Hill Cumorah, near Palmyra, New York (D&C 128:20).

chapters.n: Joseph pries up the stone with a lever and sees the plates, the Urim and Thummim, and the breastplate exactly as described, resting on two crosswise stones inside a cemented stone box.
Moroni forbids Joseph to take the plates yet; that will happen in four years. Meanwhile Joseph must return to meet him on the same day each year.
Each year Joseph meets Moroni and receives instruction about the Lord’s latter-day work and how His kingdom is to be led — four years of preparation.
Because the family was poor, they worked as day laborers wherever they could, sometimes far from home, earning a modest living.

Alvin dies in 1823. In 1825 Joseph is hired by Josiah Stoal (Stowell) to search for a rumored Spanish silver mine in Pennsylvania. After a month without success, Joseph persuades him to stop. Joseph says this episode is the source of the “money-digger” stories about him.

f.g: Usually spelled Stowell; a farmer from South Bainbridge, New York, who remained Joseph’s friend.
A township on the Susquehanna River in northern Pennsylvania, near modern Oakland.

chapters.n: Joseph boards with Isaac Hale, where he meets Emma Hale. They marry on January 18, 1827.
Emma’s family opposes the marriage, partly because of Joseph’s claimed vision, so they marry at the home of a local justice in South Bainbridge, New York. Joseph then farms with his father.

f.g: Zechariah Tarble, a justice of the peace; “squire” was a title for a local magistrate.

chapters.n: On September 22, 1827, Moroni gives Joseph the plates, Urim and Thummim, and breastplate, with a strict charge: careless neglect would bring loss, but if he did all he could, they would be protected.

f.g: removed from his calling and blessings.

chapters.n: Joseph quickly learns why: people try every trick to steal the plates. Yet they stay safe until his work is done, and he returns them to Moroni, who still had them when Joseph wrote this on May 2, 1838.

Rumors “with a thousand tongues” multiply, and persecution forces Joseph and Emma to move to Emma’s family home in Pennsylvania. Martin Harris, a respected Palmyra farmer, gives them fifty dollars — a significant sum then.
Arriving in Harmony in December 1827, Joseph begins copying characters from the plates and translating some of them with the Urim and Thummim through February 1828.

f.g: The writing on the plates was called “reformed Egyptian” (Mormon 9:32).

chapters.n: In February 1828 Martin Harris takes a copy of the characters to New York City. Joseph defers to Harris’s own account of what happened.

f.g: Then the nation’s largest city, home to Columbia College scholars.

chapters.n: Martin Harris recounts showing the characters to Professor Charles Anthon of Columbia College, who he says affirmed them and wrote a certificate. When told an angel revealed the plates, Anthon called him back. Anthon later denied endorsing them; accounts differ.

f.g: A noted classics scholar at Columbia College. Little was known about Egyptian in 1828, as hieroglyphs had only recently been deciphered.

chapters.n: Anthon tears up the certificate, says angels no longer minister, and asks to see the plates. When told some were sealed, he says, “I cannot read a sealed book” — words Latter-day Saints see as fulfilling Isaiah 29:11-12.

f.w: I cannot read a sealed book

f.g: Samuel L. Mitchill, a prominent New York physician and scholar.

chapters.n: On April 5, 1829, Oliver Cowdery, a schoolteacher who had boarded with Joseph’s parents and heard about the plates, arrives to meet Joseph.
On April 7, 1829, Joseph begins translating the Book of Mormon again with Oliver as scribe. Most of the book was translated in roughly the next three months.

f.w: he began to write for me

chapters.n: In May 1829 they go into the woods to pray about baptism, which they had read about in the translation. A heavenly messenger descends in light, lays hands on them, and ordains them.

f.w: baptism for the remission of sins

chapters.n: The messenger confers the Aaronic Priesthood, which holds keys to the ministering of angels, the gospel of repentance, and baptism by immersion. It will remain until the sons of Levi again offer righteously.

f.w: I confer the Priesthood of Aaron
until the sons of Levi do offer again an offering unto the Lord in righteousness

chapters.n: The Aaronic Priesthood cannot confer the gift of the Holy Ghost; that will come later. The messenger instructs Joseph and Oliver to baptize each other.

f.w: laying on hands for the gift of the Holy Ghost

chapters.n: They obey: Joseph baptizes Oliver, Oliver baptizes Joseph, and then each ordains the other to the Aaronic Priesthood, as commanded.

The messenger was John the Baptist, acting under Peter, James, and John, who held the Melchizedek Priesthood keys and would later confer them. Joseph would be the first Elder and Oliver the second. The date was May 15, 1829, near the Susquehanna River.
Coming out of the water, both are filled with the Holy Ghost and prophesy — Oliver of things soon to come, Joseph of the rise of the Church — rejoicing in God.

f.w: the Holy Ghost fell upon him
rejoiced in the God of our salvation

chapters.n: Their minds are opened to understand the scriptures, even difficult passages. Yet they keep their priesthood and baptism secret because of growing persecution.

f.w: the scriptures laid open to our understandings

chapters.n: Mobs threatened them — led even by church members — but Emma’s family, now friendly toward Joseph, offered protection so the translation could continue. Joseph credits divine providence.

f.w: as far as in them lay
f.g: as much as they were able.
